finding.claim: The /fetch handler passes an unvalidated, attacker-controlled query parameter directly to http.Get and returns the response body to the caller, enabling full-response SSRF to loopback, RFC-1918, and cloud metadata endpoints.
finding.sink: main.go:16 http.Get(target); response body echoed via main.go:22 io.Copy(w, resp.Body)

trace.note: ListenAndServe(":8080") binds all interfaces, so the route is public ingress
target read from query string with no validation
http.Get dispatches request to attacker-chosen URL; default client follows redirects
upstream response body streamed back to the requester

finding.guards_checked: No scheme restriction on the host (Go client only speaks http/https, so not a host control). No host allowlist: the allowed map at main.go:9-12 is never consulted on this path. No authentication on the route. No CheckRedirect or post-redirect re-validation. No RFC-1918, loopback, or link-local blocking. Exposure assumes no upstream firewall; deployment config is not in the repo.

verdict.guard_found: none. The allowed map at main.go:9-12 is only consulted in safeFetch (main.go:27), not on the /fetch path. The /fetch handler (main.go:14-23) has no validation, auth, or CheckRedirect between the query read at main.go:15 and the response copy at main.go:22.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: /fetch is registered at main.go:41, the server listens on all interfaces at main.go:43, target is read unvalidated from the query string at main.go:15, http.Get(target) runs at main.go:16 (default client follows redirects), and the upstream body is streamed to the caller at main.go:22. The only validated handler is /safe (main.go:25-38), so the unguarded /fetch route is exploitable by an unauthenticated remote attacker to reach loopback, RFC-1918, and metadata addresses, subject only to the caveat that deployment firewalls are not in the repo.
